meta.subject: Physics
meta.rendering_note: All math is KaTeX in \( ... \) delimiters, one unnested span per expression. Vectors (\( \vec E \), \( \vec F \), \( \vec p \)), \( \epsilon_0 \), the Greek-letter density symbols (\( \lambda \), \( \sigma \), \( \rho \)), the angle \( \theta \) and the micro-prefix \( \mu \) are always single KaTeX spans; no raw Unicode math symbols appear anywhere. Every numeric answer terminates cleanly or is a clean order-of-magnitude value.

topics.name: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
topics.summary: Electric charge is a basic property of matter that comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is additive: the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of its parts, with signs kept. It is conserved: rubbing or contact only moves electrons from one body to another, so the total never changes. It is quantized: every observable charge is a whole-number multiple of \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C. Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: its magnitude is \( kq_1q_2/r^{2} \) with \( k=1/4\pi\epsilon_0\approx9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), it acts along the line joining the charges, and it is repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike ones. The two forces on a pair are equal and opposite. When several charges act on one charge, the net force is the vector sum of the individual Coulomb forces, each found as if the others were absent (superposition). Always add them as vectors, never as bare magnitudes.
key_formulas: \( q=ne \), with \( n \) an integer and \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C
topics.worked_example:
Charges of \( +2\,\mu \)C and \( +3\,\mu \)C are 30 cm apart. Find the force.

\( F=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times(2\times10^{-6})(3\times10^{-6})}{(0.3)^{2}}=\dfrac{5.4\times10^{-2}}{0.09}=0.6 \) N.

Both are positive, so the force is repulsive, along the line joining them.
common_mistakes: Calling the force between like charges attractive, or between unlike charges repulsive.
Adding force magnitudes from several charges instead of adding the forces as vectors.
Forgetting to square the distance, or to convert cm and \( \mu \)C to SI units.
Adding charges without their signs when finding the total charge.

topics.name: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
topics.summary: The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there, \( \vec E=\vec F/q_0 \), with \( q_0 \) taken vanishingly small so it does not disturb the source charges. Its unit is N/C. For a point charge, \( E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}} \), falling off as \( 1/r^{2} \); the field points radially away from a positive charge and toward a negative one. A charge \( q \) placed in a field feels \( \vec F=q\vec E \), so a negative charge is pushed opposite to the field. The field of several charges is the vector sum of their separate fields (superposition), and symmetric arrangements often give zero field at a centre. Field lines picture the field: the tangent gives its direction, their crowding shows its strength, they start on positive charges and end on negative charges or at infinity, and they never cross, since the field has one direction at each point. Electrostatic field lines never form closed loops.
topics.worked_example:
Find the field 0.2 m from a \( +4\,\mu \)C charge.

\( E=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times4\times10^{-6}}{(0.2)^{2}}=\dfrac{3.6\times10^{4}}{0.04}=9\times10^{5} \) N/C.

The charge is positive, so the field points radially away from it.
common_mistakes: Drawing the field of a positive charge pointing toward it, or of a negative charge pointing away.
Using \( 1/r \) or \( 1/r^{3} \) instead of \( 1/r^{2} \) for a point charge.
Forgetting that a negative charge feels a force opposite to \( \vec E \).
Adding field magnitudes from several charges instead of adding field vectors.

topics.name: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
topics.summary: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges \( \pm q \) separated by a small distance \( 2a \). Its dipole moment \( \vec p=q(2\vec a) \) points from the negative charge toward the positive charge, with unit C m. The net charge is zero, but the field is not: far away the two fields nearly cancel, leaving a field that falls as \( 1/r^{3} \). On the axis, \( E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^{3}} \), along \( \vec p \); on the equatorial line, \( E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^{3}} \), opposite to \( \vec p \). So the axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance. In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero, but a torque \( \vec\tau=\vec p\times\vec E \), of size \( pE\sin\theta \), turns it toward the field; the torque is largest at \( 90^\circ \). Its potential energy \( U=-pE\cos\theta \) is lowest when \( \vec p \) is aligned with \( \vec E \) (stable) and highest when antiparallel. In a non-uniform field a dipole also feels a net force.
topics.worked_example:
A dipole of moment \( 4\times10^{-9} \) C m makes \( 30^\circ \) with a field of \( 5\times10^{4} \) N/C. Find the torque.

\( \tau=pE\sin30^\circ=4\times10^{-9}\times5\times10^{4}\times\tfrac12=1\times10^{-4} \) N m.

It acts to rotate \( \vec p \) into line with \( \vec E \).
common_mistakes: Drawing \( \vec p \) from the positive charge to the negative charge.
Swapping the axial and equatorial formulas, or thinking both fields are equal.
Using \( 1/r^{2} \) for the dipole far field instead of \( 1/r^{3} \).
Placing minimum potential energy at \( 90^\circ \) instead of at \( 0^\circ \).

topics.name: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
topics.summary: When charge is spread out, we describe it with a density. Linear density \( \lambda \) (C/m) is charge per unit length of a wire or ring; surface density \( \sigma \) (C/m\(^{2}\)) is charge per unit area of a sheet or shell; volume density \( \rho \) (C/m\(^{3}\)) is charge per unit volume of a solid. Total charge is density multiplied by the matching length, area or volume. Symmetry often decides the field of a distribution: for example, the field at the centre of a uniform ring is zero because opposite elements cancel. Electric flux measures how much field passes through a surface: for a flat area in a uniform field, \( \Phi=\vec E\cdot\vec A=EA\cos\theta \), where \( \theta \) is the angle between \( \vec E \) and the area vector (the normal). Its unit is N m\(^{2}\)/C. For a closed surface the area vector points outward, so field leaving gives positive flux and field entering gives negative flux. A uniform field gives zero net flux through any closed surface.
key_formulas: \( \Phi=\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A \) for a closed surface
Uniform field through a closed surface: \( \Phi=0 \)
topics.worked_example:
A field of 100 N/C crosses an area of 0.2 m\(^{2}\) whose normal makes \( 60^\circ \) with the field. Find the flux.

\( \Phi=EA\cos60^\circ=100\times0.2\times\tfrac12=10 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.
common_mistakes: Using the angle with the surface instead of the angle with the normal.
Mixing up \( \lambda \), \( \sigma \) and \( \rho \) or their units.
Adding entering and leaving flux as magnitudes instead of with signs.
Dividing by the density's length, area or volume when you should multiply.

topics.name: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
topics.summary: Gauss's law states that the total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by \( \epsilon_0 \): \( \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=q_{enc}/\epsilon_0 \). Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux, although they still affect the field at points on it. The law is always true, but it gives \( E \) easily only when symmetry makes \( E \) constant over a well-chosen Gaussian surface. Three standard results follow. An infinite line charge, using a coaxial cylinder, gives \( E=\lambda/2\pi\epsilon_0 r \). An infinite plane sheet, using a pillbox, gives \( E=\sigma/2\epsilon_0 \), independent of distance. A uniformly charged thin spherical shell gives \( E=0 \) inside and the point-charge field outside. Just outside a charged conductor the field is \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \), normal to the surface, twice the thin-sheet value, because the field inside the conductor is zero and all the flux leaves through one side. A charge at the centre of a cube sends \( q/6\epsilon_0 \) through each face. Always match the Gaussian surface to the symmetry of the charge.
key_formulas: Plane sheet: \( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} \); conductor surface: \( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} \)
Thin shell: \( E=0 \) for \( r<R \), \( E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \) for \( r>R \)
topics.worked_example:
An infinite sheet has \( \sigma=8.85\times10^{-6} \) C/m\(^{2}\). Find the field near it (\( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12} \)).

\( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-6}}{2\times8.85\times10^{-12}}=5\times10^{5} \) N/C, pointing away from the sheet on both sides.
common_mistakes: Counting charges outside the Gaussian surface in \( q_{enc} \).
Using \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) for a conductor's surface instead of \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \).
Applying the point-charge formula at a point inside a charged shell.
Pulling \( E \) out of the flux integral when the surface has no suitable symmetry.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Two small spheres, each carrying a positive charge, are held a short distance apart. What is the nature and direction of the electrostatic force each exerts on the other?
options: Repulsive, directed along the line joining the two charges
Attractive, directed along the line joining the two charges
Repulsive, directed perpendicular to the line joining the two charges
Zero, because both charges have the same sign
questions.explanation:
Coulomb's law says the force between two point charges acts along the straight line joining them.

Like charges repel, so each positively charged sphere is pushed directly away from the other along that line.
questions.hint: Recall the rule for like and unlike charges, and remember the Coulomb force is a central force.
distractor_logic: Reverses Coulomb's rule: like charges repel; only unlike charges attract.
The Coulomb force is central; it always acts along the joining line, never perpendicular to it.
Confuses 'same sign' with cancellation; like charges still exert a nonzero, repulsive force on each other.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Which of the following can NOT be the net charge on an isolated body? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
Charge is quantized: every net charge must be \( q=ne \) with \( n \) an integer.

\( 2.4\times10^{-19}/1.6\times10^{-19}=1.5 \), which is not an integer, so this charge cannot occur.

The other values give \( n=2,\,3,\,10 \), all allowed.
questions.hint: Divide each value by \( e \) and check whether you get a whole number.
distractor_logic: This equals \( 2e \), an integer multiple of \( e \), so it is allowed.
This equals \( 3e \), an integer multiple of \( e \), so it is allowed.
This equals \( 10e \); a larger power of ten does not break quantization.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A glass rod rubbed with silk acquires a charge of \( +5 \) nC. If no other objects are involved, what charge does the silk acquire?
questions.explanation:
Rubbing merely transfers electrons from one body to the other; total charge is conserved.

The system started neutral, so \( q_{glass}+q_{silk}=0 \), giving \( q_{silk}=-5 \) nC. The electrons removed from the glass now sit on the silk.
questions.hint: Total charge of the glass-silk system before rubbing was zero.
distractor_logic: Assumes both bodies end up with the same charge, which would create charge from nothing.
Assumes the silk stays neutral, ignoring that the electrons lost by the glass must go somewhere.
Doubles the transferred charge; conservation only requires the two charges to sum to zero.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: The Coulomb force between two point charges is \( F \). If the separation between them is doubled while the charges stay the same, the new force is
questions.explanation:
Coulomb's law: \( F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^{2}} \), an inverse-square law.

Replacing \( r \) by \( 2r \) multiplies the denominator by 4, so the force becomes \( F/4 \).
questions.hint: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law.
distractor_logic: Treats the force as varying as \( 1/r \) instead of \( 1/r^{2} \).
Treats force as increasing with distance, the opposite of Coulomb's law.
Uses a \( 1/r^{3} \) dependence, which belongs to a dipole's far field, not two point charges.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: How many electrons together carry a total charge of magnitude 1 C? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
Use \( q=ne \), so \( n=q/e \).

\( n=\dfrac{1}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=6.25\times10^{18} \) electrons.
questions.hint: Number of electrons equals total charge divided by the charge of one electron.
distractor_logic: Flips the sign of the exponent of \( e \) instead of actually taking the reciprocal.
Gets the digits right but gives a tiny number; a count of electrons for 1 C must be huge.
Quotes the charge of a single electron rather than the number of electrons.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Two point charges of \( 1\,\mu \)C each are placed 1 m apart in vacuum. Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), what is the magnitude of the force between them?
questions.explanation:
\( F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}}{1^{2}} \).

\( F=9\times10^{-3} \) N (the force is repulsive, since both charges are positive).
questions.hint: Convert \( \mu \)C to C for both charges before substituting.
distractor_logic: Uses the \( 10^{-6} \) factor only once instead of once for each charge.
Treats \( \mu \)C as C, ignoring the micro-prefix completely.
Leaves out Coulomb's constant \( k \), keeping only \( q_1q_2/r^{2} \).

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Three small bodies carry charges \( +3\,\mu \)C, \( -5\,\mu \)C and \( +1\,\mu \)C. What is the total charge of the system?
questions.explanation:
Charge is a scalar and is additive: signs must be kept.

\( 3+(-5)+1=-1 \), so the total charge is \( -1\,\mu \)C.
questions.hint: Add the charges as signed numbers.
distractor_logic: Adds the magnitudes, ignoring the signs; charge adds algebraically.
Gets the size right but drops the minus sign of the result.
Adds only the positive charges and ignores the negative one.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A neutral metal sphere becomes positively charged. What has happened to it?
options: It has gained some extra electrons
It has gained protons from the surroundings
Some of its electrons have turned into protons
It has lost some of its electrons
questions.explanation:
In ordinary charging only electrons move, since they are the mobile, loosely held particles.

A body turns positive when it loses electrons, leaving an excess of (fixed) positive nuclear charge.
questions.hint: Which particle is free to move from one body to another?
distractor_logic: Gaining electrons makes a body negative, not positive.
Protons are bound inside nuclei and are not transferred in ordinary charging.
Charge is conserved; electrons cannot convert into protons during charging.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: What is the direction of the electric field at a point near an isolated positive point charge?
options: Radially outward, away from the charge
Tangential, along circles centred on the charge
There is no field; a field exists only between two charges
questions.explanation:
\( \vec E \) is the force per unit positive test charge.

A positive test charge near a positive source is repelled, so \( \vec E \) points radially away from the charge.
questions.hint: Imagine a small positive test charge placed nearby: which way is it pushed?
distractor_logic: Reverses the field direction; a positive test charge is repelled by a positive source, so the field points away.
Circular lines belong to the magnetic field of a current, not the electric field of a point charge.
A single charge produces a field everywhere around it; a second charge is not required.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Why can two electric field lines never cross each other?
options: Because field lines repel each other like like charges do
At the crossing point the field would have two different directions, which is impossible
Because electric field lines always form closed loops
Because the field is zero everywhere between two lines
questions.explanation:
The tangent to a field line at a point gives the direction of \( \vec E \) there.

If two lines crossed, there would be two tangents, i.e. two directions for \( \vec E \) at one point, which cannot happen.
questions.hint: What does the tangent to a field line tell you?
distractor_logic: Treats field lines as physical objects; they are only a picture of the field.
Electrostatic field lines start and end on charges; they do not form closed loops.
The gaps between drawn lines are not regions of zero field; lines are just drawn at intervals.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric field?
questions.explanation:
By definition \( \vec E=\vec F/q_0 \).

So the unit is newton per coulomb, N/C (equivalently V/m).
questions.hint: Write down the defining relation for the field.
distractor_logic: Multiplies force by charge instead of dividing.
Inverts the definition \( \vec E=\vec F/q_0 \).
This is the unit of electric flux, not field.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: At a distance \( r \) from a point charge the field magnitude is \( E \). What is the field magnitude at distance \( 3r \)?
questions.explanation:
For a point charge \( E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}} \).

Tripling \( r \) multiplies \( r^{2} \) by 9, so the field becomes \( E/9 \).
questions.hint: The point-charge field is inverse-square.
distractor_logic: Uses a \( 1/r \) dependence instead of \( 1/r^{2} \).
Uses a \( 1/r^{3} \) dependence, which is the dipole far-field law.
Makes the field grow with distance instead of falling off.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: An electron is placed in a uniform electric field that points due east. In which direction does the electric force on the electron act?
options: It experiences no force in a uniform field
questions.explanation:
\( \vec F=q\vec E \).

For an electron \( q=-e \), so \( \vec F \) is opposite to \( \vec E \): the force points due west.
questions.hint: Watch the sign of the electron's charge in \( \vec F=q\vec E \).
distractor_logic: Forgets that the electron is negative, so \( \vec F=q\vec E \) is opposite to \( \vec E \).
The force on a charge is along or against the field, never sideways.
Confuses the zero NET force on a dipole in a uniform field with the force on a single charge.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: In a diagram of electric field lines, the lines are drawn much closer together in one region. What does this indicate?
options: The field is weaker in that region
The field is stronger in that region
The field changes direction in that region
A charge must be located in that region
questions.explanation:
The density of field lines (lines per unit area normal to them) is proportional to the magnitude of \( \vec E \).

So closely packed lines mean a strong field.
questions.hint: Think of line density as a picture of field strength.
distractor_logic: Reverses the rule; crowded lines mean a larger field magnitude.
Line spacing encodes magnitude, not a reversal of direction.
Lines crowd near charges but also anywhere the field is strong; crowding alone does not prove a charge is present there.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: For a static charge distribution, where do electric field lines begin and end?
options: They begin on negative charges and end on positive charges
They form closed loops with no beginning or end
They begin on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity)
They begin and end on the same charge
questions.explanation:
Field lines follow the direction a positive test charge would be pushed.

So they leave positive charges and terminate on negative charges; for an isolated charge they run off to infinity.
questions.hint: Which way would a positive test charge move near each type of charge?
distractor_logic: Reverses the convention; lines point away from positive and toward negative charge.
Closed loops describe magnetic field lines, not electrostatic ones.
A line leaving a charge cannot return to it; that would require a closed loop.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: What is the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of 3 m from a point charge of \( 1 \) nC? (Take \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\).)
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{kq}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times10^{-9}}{3^{2}} \).

\( E=\dfrac{9}{9}=1 \) N/C, directed away from the charge if it is positive.
questions.hint: Use \( E=kq/r^{2} \) with \( q \) in coulombs.
distractor_logic: Divides by \( r \) instead of \( r^{2} \).
Forgets to divide by \( r^{2} \) at all, leaving just \( kq \).
Divides by \( r^{3} \), a dipole-like fall-off.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: In which direction does the dipole moment \( \vec p \) of an electric dipole point?
options: From the negative charge toward the positive charge
From the positive charge toward the negative charge
Perpendicular to the line joining the two charges
It has no direction, since dipole moment is a scalar
questions.explanation:
By definition \( \vec p=q\,(2\vec a) \), where \( 2\vec a \) is the displacement from \( -q \) to \( +q \).

So \( \vec p \) points from the negative charge toward the positive charge.
questions.hint: The displacement vector in \( \vec p=q(2\vec a) \) starts at the negative charge.
distractor_logic: The classic reversal: \( \vec p \) points from \( -q \) to \( +q \), opposite to the field line joining them.
\( \vec p \) lies along the dipole axis, not across it.
Dipole moment is a vector, \( \vec p=q\,(2\vec a) \).

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric dipole moment?
questions.explanation:
\( p=q\times2a \), a charge multiplied by a length.

So its unit is coulomb metre, C m.
questions.hint: Dipole moment is charge times separation.
distractor_logic: Divides charge by length instead of multiplying.
This is the unit of torque, not of dipole moment.
Squares the length; \( p \) is charge times one length.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole consists of charges \( \pm2\,\mu \)C separated by 1 cm. What is the magnitude of its dipole moment?
questions.explanation:
\( p=q\times2a=(2\times10^{-6})\times(1\times10^{-2}) \).

\( p=2\times10^{-8} \) C m, pointing from \( -2\,\mu \)C toward \( +2\,\mu \)C.
questions.hint: Use one charge magnitude times the full separation in metres.
distractor_logic: Uses the total magnitude \( 2q \) instead of \( q \).
Treats 1 cm as 1 m, missing the \( 10^{-2} \) conversion.
Uses the half-separation \( a \) instead of the full separation \( 2a \).

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field. What is the net force on it?
questions.explanation:
The field pushes \( +q \) with \( q\vec E \) and \( -q \) with \( -q\vec E \).

These are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero (though they can form a couple giving a torque).
questions.hint: Write the force on each charge as a vector and add them.
distractor_logic: Counts the force on only one of the two charges.
Adds the magnitudes of the two forces, ignoring that they point in opposite directions.
Adds magnitudes and also picks a direction; the two forces actually cancel.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole is free to rotate in a uniform field. At what angle between \( \vec p \) and \( \vec E \) is the torque on it maximum?
questions.explanation:
\( \tau=pE\sin\theta \).

\( \sin\theta \) is largest (equal to 1) at \( \theta=90^\circ \), so the torque is maximum when \( \vec p \) is perpendicular to \( \vec E \).
questions.hint: Where is \( \sin\theta \) largest?
distractor_logic: At \( 0^\circ \) the torque is zero; this is the stable orientation, not the maximum-torque one.
At \( 180^\circ \) the torque is also zero (unstable equilibrium).
\( \sin45^\circ \) is less than 1, so the torque is not maximum there.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: For a dipole in a uniform field, which orientation is the position of stable equilibrium?
questions.explanation:
\( U=-pE\cos\theta \) is lowest (most negative) at \( \theta=0^\circ \).

Minimum potential energy with zero torque means stable equilibrium: \( \vec p \) aligned with \( \vec E \).
questions.hint: Stable equilibrium is where potential energy is minimum.
distractor_logic: At \( 180^\circ \) the torque is zero but the energy is maximum, so it is unstable.
At \( 90^\circ \) the torque is maximum, so the dipole is not even in equilibrium.
There is a nonzero torque at \( 45^\circ \), so this is not equilibrium.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: Far from an electric dipole (\( r\gg a \)), how does the magnitude of its field depend on the distance \( r \)?
questions.explanation:
Far away, the fields of \( +q \) and \( -q \) nearly cancel.

What survives is proportional to \( p/r^{3} \), both on the axis and on the equatorial line.
questions.hint: A dipole's field falls off one power faster than a point charge's.
distractor_logic: This is the point-charge law; a dipole's field falls off faster.
This is the infinite-line-charge law.
This is the infinite-sheet result.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: An electric dipole consists of charges \( +q \) and \( -q \) separated by \( 2a \). Which statement about it is correct?
options: Its net charge is zero, so it produces no electric field anywhere
Its net charge is \( 2q \), so its field is like that of a point charge \( 2q \)
Its net charge is \( q \), because only the positive charge counts
Its net charge is zero, yet it produces a nonzero electric field around it
questions.explanation:
Total charge \( =+q+(-q)=0 \).

But the charges are separated, so their fields do not cancel exactly; the result is the dipole field.
questions.hint: Add the charges with signs, then ask whether separated charges' fields cancel everywhere.
distractor_logic: Zero net charge does not mean zero field; the two charges sit at different points.
Adds magnitudes instead of signed charges.
Negative charge counts just as much as positive charge in the total.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: The linear charge density \( \lambda \) of a thin charged wire is defined as
options: Charge per unit length, measured in C/m
Charge per unit area, measured in C/m\(^{2}\)
Charge per unit volume, measured in C/m\(^{3}\)
Length per unit charge, measured in m/C
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta l} \), the charge carried per unit length of the wire.

Its SI unit is C/m.
questions.hint: Linear means 'along a line'.
distractor_logic: This is surface charge density \( \sigma \).
This is volume charge density \( \rho \).
Inverts the definition.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: Which symbol is conventionally used for volume charge density, and what is its SI unit?
questions.explanation:
Volume charge density \( \rho=\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta V} \).

Its unit is C/m\(^{3}\).
questions.hint: Match: line with \( \lambda \), surface with \( \sigma \), volume with \( \rho \).
distractor_logic: \( \sigma \) is reserved for surface charge density.
Right symbol, but per unit volume needs m\(^{3}\), not m\(^{2}\).
\( \lambda \), C/m is linear charge density.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A flat surface of area \( A \) lies in a uniform field \( \vec E \), with its normal making an angle \( \theta \) with \( \vec E \). The electric flux through it is
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=\vec E\cdot\vec A=EA\cos\theta \), where \( \vec A \) is the area vector along the normal.

Only the component of \( \vec E \) along the normal passes through the surface.
questions.hint: Flux is a dot product of \( \vec E \) with the area vector.
distractor_logic: Uses sine, which would be right only if \( \theta \) were measured from the plane itself.
Ignores orientation; flux depends on how much area faces the field.
Divides by area instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A flat surface is held in a uniform field so that its area vector is perpendicular to the field. What is the flux through it?
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=EA\cos\theta \) with \( \theta=90^\circ \).

\( \cos90^\circ=0 \), so no field lines cross the surface and the flux is zero.
questions.hint: If the area vector is perpendicular to \( \vec E \), how is the surface itself oriented?
distractor_logic: Confuses the area vector with the plane; here the field lines run parallel to the surface.
No partial factor applies; \( \cos90^\circ=0 \) exactly.
A negative flux needs the field to enter against the area vector, not run along the surface.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric flux?
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=EA \), so its unit is (N/C)(m\(^{2}\)).

That is N m\(^{2}\)/C.
questions.hint: Multiply the unit of field by the unit of area.
distractor_logic: This is the unit of electric field.
Inverts the area and charge parts of the unit.
This is the unit of surface charge density.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A thin rod 2 m long carries a charge of \( 4\,\mu \)C spread uniformly along it. What is its linear charge density?
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{Q}{L}=\dfrac{4\,\mu\text{C}}{2\text{ m}} \).

\( \lambda=2\,\mu \)C/m.
questions.hint: Charge divided by length.
distractor_logic: Multiplies charge by length instead of dividing.
Divides length by charge, inverting the definition.
Right number, wrong unit: a rod has a linear density, per metre.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A uniform field of 200 N/C passes through a flat area of 0.5 m\(^{2}\) whose normal is parallel to the field. What is the flux through the area?
questions.explanation:
Normal parallel to \( \vec E \) means \( \theta=0^\circ \), so \( \Phi=EA \).

\( \Phi=200\times0.5=100 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.
questions.hint: Use \( \Phi=EA\cos\theta \) with \( \theta=0^\circ \).
distractor_logic: Divides \( E \) by \( A \) instead of multiplying.
Confuses 'normal parallel to field' with 'surface parallel to field'.
Right number, but N/C is the unit of field, not flux.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: For a closed surface, in which direction is the area vector of each small surface element taken?
options: Along the inward normal to the surface
Along the direction of the external field
Along the outward normal to the surface
questions.explanation:
For a closed surface the convention is that \( d\vec A \) points along the outward normal.

That is why field lines leaving a surface give positive flux and those entering give negative flux.
questions.hint: Leaving lines count as positive flux by convention.
distractor_logic: The convention is outward; inward would flip the sign of every flux.
An area vector is always normal to the surface, never tangent.
The area vector depends only on the surface's geometry, not on the field.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface equals
options: \( q_{enc}/\epsilon_0 \), where \( q_{enc} \) is the net charge enclosed by the surface
\( q_{total}/\epsilon_0 \), counting all charges both inside and outside the surface
questions.explanation:
Gauss's law: \( \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{enc}}{\epsilon_0} \).

Only the net charge inside the closed surface appears on the right-hand side.
questions.hint: Which charges does the right-hand side of Gauss's law include?
distractor_logic: Charges outside contribute zero net flux; only enclosed charge counts.
Multiplies by \( \epsilon_0 \) instead of dividing.
This mixes up flux with the field of a point charge.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A charge \( +q \) sits at the centre of a spherical surface of radius \( R \). If the radius of the surface is doubled, the total flux through it
questions.explanation:
By Gauss's law the flux depends only on the enclosed charge.

Field falls as \( 1/r^{2} \) while area grows as \( r^{2} \), so their product stays \( q/\epsilon_0 \).
questions.hint: Has the enclosed charge changed?
distractor_logic: Accounts for the field falling as \( 1/r^{2} \) but forgets the area growing as \( r^{2} \).
Accounts for the larger area but forgets the weaker field.
Uses a \( 1/r \) scaling that has no basis here.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A point charge \( q \) lies outside a closed surface. What is the net flux through the surface due to this charge?
options: Negative, because its field lines enter the surface
questions.explanation:
Every field line from an outside charge that enters the surface also leaves it.

Entering (negative) and leaving (positive) flux cancel, so the net flux is zero, consistent with \( q_{enc}=0 \).
questions.hint: Follow a field line from the outside charge through the surface.
distractor_logic: Treats an outside charge as if it were enclosed.
Invents a partial share; an outside charge contributes nothing net.
Counts only the entering lines; the same lines also leave, giving equal positive flux.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A thin spherical shell of radius \( R \) carries a charge \( Q \) spread uniformly over it. What is the electric field at a point inside the shell (\( r<R \))?
options: Infinite at the centre, decreasing outward
questions.explanation:
Take a concentric Gaussian sphere of radius \( r
By symmetry \( E \) is the same everywhere on it, so \( E\cdot4\pi r^{2}=0 \), giving \( E=0 \) inside.
questions.hint: How much charge does a Gaussian sphere inside the shell enclose?
distractor_logic: Applies the point-charge formula inside the shell, where it does not hold.
Uses the field value at the surface for points inside.
Treats the shell's charge as if it were concentrated at the centre.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: How does the field of an infinitely long, uniformly charged straight wire vary with perpendicular distance \( r \) from it?
questions.explanation:
Gauss's law with a coaxial cylinder gives \( E(2\pi rl)=\lambda l/\epsilon_0 \).

So \( E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r} \), which varies as \( 1/r \).
questions.hint: The curved area of a coaxial cylinder grows as \( r \).
distractor_logic: This is the point-charge law.
This is the dipole far-field law.
This is the infinite-sheet result.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: What is the field near an infinite plane sheet carrying uniform surface charge density \( \sigma \)?
questions.explanation:
Use a pillbox crossing the sheet: flux leaves through both faces, \( 2EA=\sigma A/\epsilon_0 \).

So \( E=\sigma/2\epsilon_0 \), the same at all distances.
questions.hint: A thin isolated sheet sends field out on both sides.
distractor_logic: This is the field just outside a charged conductor, where all field emerges from one side.
The sheet's field does not weaken with distance.
Borrows the point-charge form; an infinite sheet is not a point charge.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: Which Gaussian surface is most convenient for finding the field of an infinitely long uniform line charge?
options: A sphere centred on the line
A cube with the line running along one edge
A cylinder coaxial with the line
A flat plane containing the line
questions.explanation:
The line charge has cylindrical symmetry: \( E \) is radial and depends only on \( r \).

On a coaxial cylinder \( E \) is constant on the curved surface and the end caps give zero flux.
questions.hint: Match the Gaussian surface to the symmetry of the charge.
distractor_logic: A sphere does not match the cylindrical symmetry, so \( E \) is not constant over it.
The field is not constant or simply oriented over the faces of a cube.
A plane is not a closed surface, so Gauss's law cannot be applied to it.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has surface charge density \( \sigma \) at a certain point. What is the electric field just outside the surface there?
options: Zero, since the field in a conductor is zero
questions.explanation:
A pillbox straddling the surface has flux only through its outer face, since \( E=0 \) inside.

\( EA=\sigma A/\epsilon_0 \), so \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0 \), directed along the normal.
questions.hint: Compare with an isolated sheet: how many faces of the pillbox carry flux here?
distractor_logic: Uses the thin isolated sheet formula; for a conductor the field inside is zero, so all of it emerges outward.
A tangential field would move surface charges, so equilibrium demands a normal field.
The field is zero inside the material, not just outside the surface.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Charges of \( +2\,\mu \)C and \( +3\,\mu \)C are placed 30 cm apart in vacuum. Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), find the force between them.
questions.explanation:
\( F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times(2\times10^{-6})(3\times10^{-6})}{(0.3)^{2}} \).

\( F=\dfrac{5.4\times10^{-2}}{0.09}=0.6 \) N.

Both charges are positive, so the force is repulsive.
questions.hint: Convert 30 cm to metres and square it.
distractor_logic: Gets the size right but reverses the nature; like charges repel.
Divides by \( r \) instead of \( r^{2} \).
Substitutes 30 m instead of 0.30 m for the separation.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Two point charges attract each other with force \( F \). If both charges are doubled and their separation is also doubled, the new force is
questions.explanation:
\( F\propto\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}} \).

Doubling both charges multiplies the numerator by 4; doubling \( r \) multiplies the denominator by 4.

The two effects cancel, so the force stays \( F \).
questions.hint: Track the factor from the charges and from \( r^{2} \) separately.
distractor_logic: Accounts for doubling the charges but forgets the larger separation.
Accounts for the larger separation but forgets doubling the charges.
Treats force as proportional to charge and inversely to distance, both linearly.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Charges \( +q \) are fixed at \( x=0 \) and at \( x=2d \). A third charge \( +q_0 \) is placed at \( x=d \). What is the net Coulomb force on \( q_0 \)?
questions.explanation:
The charge at \( x=0 \) pushes \( q_0 \) along \( +x \) with \( kqq_0/d^{2} \).

The charge at \( x=2d \) pushes it along \( -x \) with the same magnitude.

The vector sum is zero.
questions.hint: Draw both force arrows on \( q_0 \) before adding.
distractor_logic: Adds the two force magnitudes instead of adding them as vectors.
Counts only the force from one of the charges.
Uses the full distance \( 2d \) and counts only one charge.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Two identical small conducting spheres carry \( +6\,\mu \)C and \( -2\,\mu \)C. They are touched together and returned to their original separation. How does the force between them change?
options: It becomes one-third as strong and stays attractive
Its magnitude is unchanged, but it becomes repulsive
It becomes zero, because the charges neutralise each other
It becomes one-third as strong and changes from attractive to repulsive
questions.explanation:
On contact the total \( +6-2=+4\,\mu \)C is shared equally: each gets \( +2\,\mu \)C.

Before: \( |q_1q_2|=12 \); after: \( q_1q_2=4 \), so the force is one-third as large.

Both are now positive, so the force is repulsive instead of attractive.
questions.hint: Conservation of charge first, then equal sharing between identical spheres.
distractor_logic: After sharing, both spheres carry the same positive charge, so they repel.
Ignores the change in the charges' magnitudes; the product drops from 12 to 4.
Only part of the charge cancels; the net \( +4\,\mu \)C is shared, \( +2\,\mu \)C each.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: For two electrons, roughly how large is the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between them (for any separation)?
questions.explanation:
Both forces vary as \( 1/r^{2} \), so the ratio is \( \dfrac{ke^{2}}{Gm_e^{2}} \), independent of distance.

Numerically this is about \( 4\times10^{42} \): electric forces vastly dominate between charged particles.
questions.hint: Both forces are inverse-square, so the separation cancels in the ratio.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; gravity is the far weaker force.
Assumes the two forces are comparable.
Takes the ratio as just the size of \( k \), ignoring \( G \) and the masses.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: The force on charge \( q_1 \) due to charge \( q_2 \) is \( \vec F_{12} \). What is the force \( \vec F_{21} \) on \( q_2 \) due to \( q_1 \)?
options: Zero, since only one charge can exert the force
questions.explanation:
Coulomb forces obey Newton's third law.

\( \vec F_{21} \) has the same magnitude as \( \vec F_{12} \), acts along the same line, and points the opposite way: \( \vec F_{21}=-\vec F_{12} \).
questions.hint: Think action and reaction.
distractor_logic: Gets the magnitude but not the direction; the forces point oppositely along the line.
Both charges exert forces on each other.
There is no factor of 2; magnitudes are equal.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A charge of \( +1\,\mu \)C is at the origin and \( +4\,\mu \)C is at \( x=0.3 \) m. Where on the x-axis should a third charge be placed so that the net force on it is zero?
options: At \( x=0.2 \) m, between the two charges
At \( x=0.06 \) m, between the two charges
At \( x=0.1 \) m, between the two charges
At \( x=-0.1 \) m, outside the pair on the side of the smaller charge
questions.explanation:
For like charges the forces can cancel only between them. Let the point be at \( x \).

\( \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}=\dfrac{4}{(0.3-x)^{2}} \Rightarrow 0.3-x=2x \Rightarrow x=0.1 \) m.
questions.hint: Balance point lies nearer the smaller charge, with distances in the ratio of the square roots of the charges.
distractor_logic: Places the point nearer the larger charge; it must lie nearer the smaller one.
Uses the ratio of charges (1:4) for the distances instead of its square root (1:2).
Outside two like charges the two forces point the same way, so they cannot cancel.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A body acquires a charge of \( +3.2\,\mu \)C. How many electrons were transferred, and in which direction? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
\( n=\dfrac{q}{e}=\dfrac{3.2\times10^{-6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=2\times10^{13} \).

A positive charge means electrons were removed.
questions.hint: Use \( n=q/e \) and let the sign decide the direction of transfer.
distractor_logic: Adding electrons would make the body negative.
Ignores the micro-prefix, dividing 3.2 C by \( e \).
Divides \( e \) by \( q \), producing an impossible fractional count.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Find the electric field at a point 0.2 m from a point charge of \( +4\,\mu \)C. (Take \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\).)
options: \( 9\times10^{5} \) N/C, directed away from the charge
\( 1.8\times10^{5} \) N/C, directed away from the charge
\( 4.5\times10^{6} \) N/C, directed away from the charge
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{kq}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times4\times10^{-6}}{(0.2)^{2}}=\dfrac{3.6\times10^{4}}{0.04} \).

\( E=9\times10^{5} \) N/C, pointing away from the positive charge.
questions.hint: Square the distance, and remember which way a positive charge's field points.
distractor_logic: Reverses the direction; the field of a positive charge points outward.
Divides by \( r \) instead of \( r^{2} \).
Divides by \( r^{3} \) instead of \( r^{2} \).

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Equal charges \( +q \) are fixed at \( x=-a \) and \( x=+a \). What is the electric field at the origin?
questions.explanation:
The charge at \( -a \) gives a field along \( +x \) at the origin; the one at \( +a \) gives an equal field along \( -x \).

They cancel, so \( \vec E=0 \) at the midpoint.
questions.hint: Draw each field arrow at the origin, pointing away from its source charge.
distractor_logic: Adds the two field magnitudes instead of adding the vectors.
Counts only one charge's field.
Uses the separation \( 2a \) and adds the two magnitudes.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A charge \( +q \) is at \( x=0 \) and \( -q \) is at \( x=d \). What is the electric field at the midpoint?
questions.explanation:
Each charge is \( d/2 \) away, giving magnitude \( \dfrac{kq}{(d/2)^{2}}=\dfrac{4kq}{d^{2}} \).

Field of \( +q \) points away from it (toward \( -q \)); field of \( -q \) points toward it. Both point the same way.

Net: \( 8kq/d^{2} \) toward \( -q \).
questions.hint: For opposite charges, check whether the two fields at the midpoint point the same way.
distractor_logic: Assumes cancellation as for equal like charges; for opposite charges the fields add.
Reverses both fields; field points away from \( +q \) and toward \( -q \).
Counts the field of only one charge.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A proton is placed in a uniform field of \( 2\times10^{4} \) N/C. What force acts on it? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
\( F=qE=(1.6\times10^{-19})(2\times10^{4})=3.2\times10^{-15} \) N.

The proton is positive, so the force is along \( \vec E \).
questions.hint: \( \vec F=q\vec E \) with a positive \( q \).
distractor_logic: Gives the direction for an electron, not a proton.
Divides \( E \) by \( e \) instead of multiplying.
Confuses the field value with the force.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: The field is defined as \( \vec E=\vec F/q_0 \) in the limit \( q_0\to0 \). Why is the test charge taken to be vanishingly small?
options: So that the test charge does not disturb the source charges that produce the field
Because a finite test charge would make the field infinite
So that the force becomes zero and the field can be defined as zero
Because the field direction is defined using a negative test charge
questions.explanation:
A real test charge can push the source charges around (for example, redistributing charge on a conductor).

Taking \( q_0\to0 \) makes this disturbance negligible, so \( \vec E \) describes the source alone.
questions.hint: What could a large test charge do to the charges it is probing?
distractor_logic: A finite test charge gives a finite force; the issue is disturbance, not divergence.
The ratio \( F/q_0 \) stays finite even as both shrink.
The convention uses a positive test charge.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A charge \( +q \) is at \( x=0 \) and \( -4q \) is at \( x=0.5 \) m. Where on the x-axis is the electric field zero?
options: At \( x=0.1 \) m, between the charges
At \( x=-0.5 \) m, on the side of \( +q \) away from \( -4q \)
At \( x=1.0 \) m, beyond the \( -4q \) charge
Nowhere; opposite charges never produce a zero-field point
questions.explanation:
The null point lies outside the pair, near the smaller charge. Let it be a distance \( x \) from \( +q \).

\( \dfrac{q}{x^{2}}=\dfrac{4q}{(x+0.5)^{2}} \Rightarrow x+0.5=2x \Rightarrow x=0.5 \) m, i.e. at \( x=-0.5 \) m.
questions.hint: For unlike charges, look outside the pair on the side of the smaller charge.
distractor_logic: Between opposite charges the two fields point the same way, so they cannot cancel.
Beyond the larger charge its field always dominates.
A null point exists outside the pair, nearer the smaller charge.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: How do the electric field lines of an isolated negative point charge look?
options: Straight radial lines pointing outward from the charge
Concentric circles centred on the charge
Straight radial lines pointing inward, converging on the charge
Curved lines leaving and returning to the charge
questions.explanation:
A positive test charge near a negative source is pulled toward it.

So the lines are radial and point inward, ending on the negative charge.
questions.hint: Which way is a positive test charge pulled?
distractor_logic: Reverses the direction; lines end on negative charges.
Circles would mean no radial force, which is wrong for a point charge.
Electrostatic lines do not loop back to their own charge.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A tiny drop carrying charge \( +3.2\times10^{-19} \) C is held stationary in a uniform field of magnitude \( 1\times10^{5} \) N/C. What is the weight of the drop, and which way must the field point?
options: \( 3.2\times10^{-14} \) N; the field points vertically downward
\( 3.2\times10^{-24} \) N; the field points vertically upward
\( 1.6\times10^{-14} \) N; the field points vertically upward
\( 3.2\times10^{-14} \) N; the field points vertically upward
questions.explanation:
Balance: \( qE=mg \), so the weight equals \( qE=(3.2\times10^{-19})(1\times10^{5})=3.2\times10^{-14} \) N.

The electric force must point up; for a positive charge that needs \( \vec E \) pointing upward.
questions.hint: Electric force must balance weight exactly.
distractor_logic: A downward field would push a positive charge down, adding to its weight.
Divides \( q \) by \( E \) instead of multiplying.
Uses \( e \) instead of the given \( 2e \).

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: At the same large distance \( r \) from a short dipole, what is the ratio of the field magnitude on its axis to that on its equatorial line?
questions.explanation:
\( E_{axial}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^{3}} \) and \( E_{equatorial}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^{3}} \).

So the ratio is \( 2:1 \).
questions.hint: Recall which formula carries the factor 2.
distractor_logic: Swaps the axial and equatorial formulas.
Assumes the dipole field is the same in all directions.
Cubes the factor of 2, confusing it with the \( 1/r^{3} \) law.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole of moment \( 4\times10^{-9} \) C m makes \( 30^\circ \) with a uniform field of \( 5\times10^{4} \) N/C. Find the torque on it.
options: \( 1\times10^{-4} \) N m, tending to rotate \( \vec p \) away from \( \vec E \)
\( 1\times10^{-4} \) N m, tending to rotate \( \vec p \) into line with \( \vec E \)
\( \sqrt{3}\times10^{-4} \) N m, tending to rotate \( \vec p \) into line with \( \vec E \)
\( 2\times10^{-4} \) N m, tending to rotate \( \vec p \) into line with \( \vec E \)
questions.explanation:
\( \tau=pE\sin\theta=(4\times10^{-9})(5\times10^{4})(\tfrac12) \).

\( \tau=1\times10^{-4} \) N m, acting to align \( \vec p \) with \( \vec E \).
questions.hint: \( \vec\tau=\vec p\times\vec E \).
distractor_logic: Reverses the sense; the torque turns the dipole toward the field, the stable orientation.
Uses \( \cos30^\circ \) instead of \( \sin30^\circ \).
Drops the \( \sin\theta \) factor, giving the maximum torque.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: At a point on the equatorial line of a short dipole, in which direction does the electric field point?
options: Perpendicular to \( \vec p \), directed away from the dipole
Nowhere, since the point is equidistant from both charges and the field is zero
questions.explanation:
On the equatorial line the two fields have equal magnitude; their components along the perpendicular bisector cancel.

Their components parallel to the axis add and point from \( +q \) toward \( -q \), i.e. opposite to \( \vec p \).
questions.hint: Sketch both field arrows at a point on the bisector and resolve them.
distractor_logic: Parallel to \( \vec p \) is the axial-line direction.
The radial components of the two fields cancel; only the part along the axis survives.
Equal distances give equal magnitudes, but the fields do not cancel; their axial components add.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: The field at a point far out on a dipole's axis is \( E \). If the distance from the dipole's centre is doubled, the field becomes
questions.explanation:
Far from a dipole \( E\propto1/r^{3} \).

Doubling \( r \) divides the field by \( 2^{3}=8 \).
questions.hint: Dipole far fields fall off as the cube of distance.
distractor_logic: Uses the point-charge \( 1/r^{2} \) law.
Uses a \( 1/r \) law.
Uses a \( 1/r^{4} \) law.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole of moment \( 2\times10^{-8} \) C m makes \( 60^\circ \) with a uniform field of \( 1\times10^{4} \) N/C. What is its potential energy?
questions.explanation:
\( U=-pE\cos\theta=-(2\times10^{-8})(1\times10^{4})\cos60^\circ \).

\( U=-2\times10^{-4}\times\tfrac12=-1\times10^{-4} \) J.
questions.hint: Energy uses cosine and carries a minus sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the minus sign in \( U=-pE\cos\theta \).
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) in place of \( \cos60^\circ \).
Leaves out the \( \cos\theta \) factor.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: How much work must an external agent do to rotate a dipole slowly from \( \theta=0^\circ \) to \( \theta=180^\circ \) in a uniform field \( E \)?
options: Zero, since the dipole ends up along a field line again
questions.explanation:
\( W=U_f-U_i=(-pE\cos180^\circ)-(-pE\cos0^\circ) \).

\( W=pE+pE=2pE \).
questions.hint: Work by the agent equals the change in potential energy.
distractor_logic: Computes the work only up to \( 90^\circ \).
Equal alignment with the field line does not mean equal energy; antiparallel has higher energy.
Sign error: the external agent must do positive work to reach the higher-energy state.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole is placed in a non-uniform electric field. In general, what does it experience?
options: Only a torque, never a net force
Only a net force, never a torque
Both a net force and a torque
Neither a force nor a torque
questions.explanation:
In a non-uniform field, \( +q \) and \( -q \) sit where \( \vec E \) differs, so the forces do not cancel: a net force.

Unless \( \vec p \) happens to lie along the field, there is also a torque.
questions.hint: Would the forces on the two ends be equal in magnitude if the field varies?
distractor_logic: This is the uniform-field result; in a non-uniform field the forces on the two ends differ.
The two forces still generally form a couple as well.
Zero net charge does not guarantee zero force in a non-uniform field.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: Dipole A has charges \( \pm1\,\mu \)C separated by 4 cm. Dipole B has charges \( \pm2\,\mu \)C separated by 1 cm. How do their dipole moments compare?
options: B's dipole moment is twice A's
A's dipole moment is four times B's
A's dipole moment is twice B's
questions.hint: Multiply charge by separation for each.
distractor_logic: Looks only at the charges, ignoring separation.
Assumes charge and separation compensate exactly.
Looks only at the separations, ignoring the charges.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A uniform field of 100 N/C passes through a flat area of 0.2 m\(^{2}\) whose normal makes \( 60^\circ \) with the field. Find the flux.
questions.explanation:
\( \Phi=EA\cos\theta=100\times0.2\times\cos60^\circ \).

\( \Phi=20\times\tfrac12=10 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.
questions.hint: The angle is measured from the normal, so use cosine.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) instead of \( \cos60^\circ \).
Ignores the angle altogether.
Divides \( E \) by \( A \) instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A closed cube of side \( a \) sits in a uniform electric field \( E \) directed perpendicular to two of its faces. What is the net flux through the cube?
questions.explanation:
Flux entering one face is \( -Ea^{2} \); flux leaving the opposite face is \( +Ea^{2} \).

The other four faces are parallel to \( \vec E \) and carry no flux. Net: zero.
questions.hint: Entering flux is negative, leaving flux is positive.
distractor_logic: Counts only the exit face.
Assumes every face carries flux \( Ea^{2} \) and adds them.
Adds the entering and leaving flux as magnitudes instead of with signs.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A solid sphere of radius \( R \) carries a total charge \( Q \) spread uniformly through its volume. What is its volume charge density?
questions.explanation:
\( \rho=\dfrac{Q}{V} \) with \( V=\dfrac43\pi R^{3} \).

\( \rho=\dfrac{3Q}{4\pi R^{3}} \).
questions.hint: Charge divided by the sphere's volume.
distractor_logic: Divides by the surface area, giving a surface density.
Multiplies by the volume instead of dividing.
Uses the right factor but the wrong power of \( R \).

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A hemispherical bowl of radius \( R \) (open, curved surface only) sits in a uniform field \( E \) parallel to its axis of symmetry. What is the magnitude of flux through the curved surface?
questions.explanation:
Close the bowl with its flat circular face. The closed surface has zero net flux.

So the curved surface carries flux equal in magnitude to that through the flat face: \( E\pi R^{2} \).
questions.hint: Imagine capping the bowl with a flat disc.
distractor_logic: Multiplies \( E \) by the curved area, ignoring that most of it is tilted to the field.
Uses a full sphere's area.
Zero net flux applies to closed surfaces; the bowl alone is open.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A square sheet of side 0.2 m carries a uniform surface charge density of \( 5\,\mu \)C/m\(^{2}\). What is its total charge?
questions.hint: Total charge equals surface density times area.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by the side length instead of the area.
Divides \( \sigma \) by the area instead of multiplying.
Multiplies by the perimeter (0.8 m) instead of the area.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: Field lines enter a closed surface through a certain patch of it. What is the sign of the flux through that patch?
options: Positive, since flux is always positive
Negative, since \( \vec E \) points against the outward area vector
Zero, since entering lines do not count
Undefined, since flux is defined only for a whole closed surface
questions.explanation:
The outward normal points out of the surface while \( \vec E \) points in.

The angle between them exceeds \( 90^\circ \), so \( \vec E\cdot d\vec A<0 \): negative flux.
questions.hint: Compare the directions of \( \vec E \) and the outward normal.
distractor_logic: Flux is a dot product and can be negative.
Entering lines contribute negative flux; they definitely count.
Flux is defined for any surface, open or closed.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A closed cylinder of radius \( R \) and length \( L \) sits in a uniform field \( E \) parallel to its axis. What is the flux through the end cap where the field enters?
questions.explanation:
The entering cap's outward normal is antiparallel to \( \vec E \), so \( \Phi=-EA \).

\( A=\pi R^{2} \), giving \( -\pi R^{2}E \). (The other cap gives \( +\pi R^{2}E \); the curved surface gives zero.)
questions.hint: Which way does the outward normal of the entry cap point?
distractor_logic: Forgets that the entering cap's outward normal opposes the field.
The curved surface carries zero flux, not the end caps.
Uses the curved-surface area instead of the cap's area.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A thin ring of radius \( R \) carries a total charge \( Q \) spread uniformly around it. What is its linear charge density?
questions.explanation:
The ring's length is its circumference, \( 2\pi R \).

\( \lambda=\dfrac{Q}{2\pi R} \).
questions.hint: Linear density: charge divided by length of the ring.
distractor_logic: Divides by the enclosed area, not the length of the ring.
Uses half the circumference.
Multiplies by the length instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A closed sphere encloses charges of \( +2\,\mu \)C and \( -5\,\mu \)C. A charge of \( +7\,\mu \)C lies outside it. What is the total flux through the sphere?
questions.explanation:
Only enclosed charge counts: \( q_{enc}=+2-5=-3\,\mu \)C.

\( \Phi=q_{enc}/\epsilon_0=-\dfrac{3\times10^{-6}}{\epsilon_0} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.
questions.hint: Ignore every charge outside the surface.
distractor_logic: Includes the outside \( +7\,\mu \)C charge, which contributes no net flux.
Drops the sign of the enclosed charge.
Multiplies by \( \epsilon_0 \) instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A point charge \( q \) is at the centre of a cube. What is the flux through any one face?
questions.explanation:
Total flux through the cube is \( q/\epsilon_0 \).

By symmetry all six faces share it equally: \( q/6\epsilon_0 \) each.
questions.hint: Six identical faces, one symmetric charge.
distractor_logic: This is the flux through the whole cube, not one face.
Multiplies by 6 instead of dividing.
Confuses the flux with the constant in the point-charge field formula.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: An infinite straight wire carries \( \lambda=+2\,\mu \)C/m. Find the field 0.2 m from it. (Use \( E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}=\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r} \) with \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\).)
options: \( 9\times10^{4} \) N/C, radially outward from the wire
\( 9\times10^{5} \) N/C, radially outward from the wire
\( 1.8\times10^{5} \) N/C, radially outward from the wire
\( 1.8\times10^{5} \) N/C, radially inward toward the wire
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}=\dfrac{2\times9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-6}}{0.2} \).

\( E=\dfrac{3.6\times10^{4}}{0.2}=1.8\times10^{5} \) N/C, pointing away from the positively charged wire.
questions.hint: Line-charge field varies as \( 1/r \), not \( 1/r^{2} \).
distractor_logic: Drops the factor 2 in \( 2k\lambda/r \).
Divides by \( r^{2} \), using a point-charge dependence.
Reverses the direction for a positive line charge.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A thin spherical shell of radius \( R \) has field \( E_s \) just outside its surface. What is the field at distance \( 2R \) from its centre?
questions.explanation:
Outside the shell it acts like a point charge at its centre: \( E\propto1/r^{2} \).

Going from \( R \) to \( 2R \) divides the field by 4.
questions.hint: Outside a shell, use the point-charge law.
distractor_logic: Uses a \( 1/r \) fall-off.
Applies the inside-the-shell result to a point outside.
Uses a \( 1/r^{3} \) fall-off.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: An infinite plane sheet carries \( \sigma=8.85\times10^{-6} \) C/m\(^{2}\). Taking \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12} \) C\(^{2}\)/(N m\(^{2}\)), find the field near it.
options: \( 5\times10^{5} \) N/C, directed away from the sheet
\( 1\times10^{6} \) N/C, directed away from the sheet
\( 2.5\times10^{5} \) N/C, directed away from the sheet
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-6}}{2\times8.85\times10^{-12}} \).

\( E=5\times10^{5} \) N/C, pointing away from the positive sheet on both sides.
questions.hint: An isolated sheet sends its field out on both sides.
distractor_logic: Uses the conductor-surface formula \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) for a thin isolated sheet.
Reverses the direction for a positive sheet.
Divides by \( 4\epsilon_0 \), an extra factor of 2 with no basis.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A charged conductor has surface charge density \( \sigma=8.85\times10^{-7} \) C/m\(^{2}\) at a point on its surface. Taking \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12} \) C\(^{2}\)/(N m\(^{2}\)), what is the field just outside that point?
questions.explanation:
Just outside a conductor \( E=\sigma/\epsilon_0 \), normal to the surface.

\( E=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-7}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=1\times10^{5} \) N/C.
questions.hint: Inside the conductor \( E=0 \), so all the pillbox flux leaves through one face.
distractor_logic: Uses the isolated-sheet formula \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) for a conductor's surface.
Zero field holds inside the conductor, not just outside.
A tangential field would drive surface currents; equilibrium needs a normal field.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: Gauss's law is true for every closed surface. For which of these can it ALONE readily give the field \( E \)?
options: A charged rod 10 cm long, at a point near one of its ends
A uniformly charged square plate, at a point near one corner
An infinitely long, uniformly charged straight wire
Two unequal point charges, at a point between them
questions.explanation:
To pull \( E \) out of \( \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A \) we need a surface over which \( E \) is constant and simply oriented.

Only the infinite wire provides this (cylindrical symmetry). The others need direct superposition.
questions.hint: Look for spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry.
distractor_logic: A finite rod lacks the symmetry needed for \( E \) to be constant over any simple Gaussian surface.
Near a corner there is no symmetry to fix the magnitude and direction of \( E \) on a surface.
Superposition, not Gauss's law, is the tool; no surface has constant \( E \) here.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A point charge sits just outside a closed spherical surface. Which statement is correct?
options: The net flux through the sphere is zero, and the field is zero at every point on the sphere
The net flux through the sphere equals \( q/\epsilon_0 \)
The net flux through the sphere is negative, since lines enter it
The net flux through the sphere is zero, but the field at points on the sphere is not zero
questions.explanation:
Gauss's law involves only enclosed charge, so the net flux is zero.

But the outside charge still produces a field everywhere on the surface; the positive and negative contributions to the flux merely cancel.
questions.hint: Distinguish total flux from the field at individual points.
distractor_logic: Zero net flux does not imply zero field; the outside charge still produces a field on the surface.
The charge is not enclosed, so it gives no net flux.
Lines that enter also leave, so the net flux is zero.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Three charges of \( +1\,\mu \)C each sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.1 m. Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), find the net force on any one charge.
options: \( 0.9\sqrt{3} \) N, directed away from the centre of the triangle
\( 1.8 \) N, directed away from the centre of the triangle
\( 0.9\sqrt{3} \) N, directed toward the centre of the triangle
\( 0.9 \) N, directed away from the centre of the triangle
questions.explanation:
Each pair force: \( F=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times10^{-12}}{(0.1)^{2}}=0.9 \) N, repulsive.

The two forces on a charge are \( 60^\circ \) apart, symmetric about the bisector, so each makes \( 30^\circ \) with it.

Net \( =2F\cos30^\circ=0.9\sqrt{3} \) N, along the bisector away from the centre.
questions.hint: Resolve both forces along the angle bisector at that corner.
distractor_logic: Adds the two force magnitudes, ignoring the \( 60^\circ \) angle between them.
Reverses the direction; like charges push each other outward.
Resolves with \( \cos60^\circ \) instead of \( \cos30^\circ \) about the bisector.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Four equal charges \( +q \) sit at the corners of a square of side \( a \). What is the net force on any one of them? (\( k=1/4\pi\epsilon_0 \))
options: \( \dfrac{kq^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(2+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \), along the diagonal, away from the centre
\( \dfrac{kq^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(\sqrt{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \), along the diagonal, away from the centre
\( \dfrac{kq^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right) \), along the diagonal, away from the centre
\( \dfrac{kq^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(\sqrt{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \), along the diagonal, toward the centre
questions.explanation:
The two adjacent charges each push with \( kq^{2}/a^{2} \) at right angles: resultant \( \sqrt2\,kq^{2}/a^{2} \) along the diagonal.

The opposite corner, \( \sqrt2a \) away, pushes along the same diagonal with \( kq^{2}/2a^{2} \).

Total: \( \dfrac{kq^{2}}{a^{2}}\left(\sqrt2+\tfrac12\right) \), outward along the diagonal.
questions.hint: Combine the two side forces first; the diagonal force is already along their resultant.
distractor_logic: Adds the two perpendicular side forces as magnitudes instead of vectors.
Takes the diagonal distance as \( a \) instead of \( \sqrt{2}a \).
Reverses the direction; all forces are repulsive.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Charges \( +2\,\mu \)C at \( x=0 \), \( -2\,\mu \)C at \( x=0.1 \) m and \( +1\,\mu \)C at \( x=0.2 \) m lie on a line. Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), find the net force on the \( +1\,\mu \)C charge.
options: \( 1.35 \) N, along \( +x \) (away from the other charges)
\( 0.45 \) N, along \( +x \) (away from the other charges)
questions.explanation:
From \( +2\,\mu \)C (0.2 m away): \( \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-12}}{0.04}=0.45 \) N, repulsive, along \( +x \).

From \( -2\,\mu \)C (0.1 m away): \( \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-12}}{0.01}=1.8 \) N, attractive, along \( -x \).

Net: \( 1.8-0.45=1.35 \) N along \( -x \).
questions.hint: Find each force with its direction, then add with signs.
distractor_logic: Adds the two force magnitudes although they point in opposite directions.
Gets the magnitude right but lets the smaller repulsion win.
Counts only the repulsion from the farther \( +2\,\mu \)C charge.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Charges \( +q \) and \( +4q \) are held a distance \( L \) apart. A third charge \( Q \) is to be placed so that all three charges are in equilibrium. What must \( Q \) be, and where?
questions.explanation:
For \( Q \) to feel zero force: \( \dfrac{q}{x^{2}}=\dfrac{4q}{(L-x)^{2}} \Rightarrow L-x=2x \Rightarrow x=L/3 \).

For \( +q \) to be balanced, \( Q \) must attract it: \( \dfrac{k|Q|q}{(L/3)^{2}}=\dfrac{k(4q)q}{L^{2}} \Rightarrow |Q|=\dfrac{4q}{9} \), and \( Q \) is negative.
questions.hint: First find where \( Q \) itself is balanced, then balance one of the outer charges.
distractor_logic: A positive middle charge would push both outer charges outward, so they could not be balanced.
Places it nearer the larger charge; balance needs it nearer the smaller one.
Uses the ratio of charges, not of their square roots, to locate the point.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Identical small conducting spheres A and B, each with charge \( Q \), repel with force \( F \). A third identical uncharged sphere C touches A, then B, and is removed. What is the new force between A and B?
questions.explanation:
C touches A: both get \( Q/2 \).

C (with \( Q/2 \)) touches B (with \( Q \)): the \( 3Q/2 \) is shared, \( 3Q/4 \) each.

New force \( \propto\dfrac{Q}{2}\cdot\dfrac{3Q}{4}=\dfrac38Q^{2} \), so it is \( 3F/8 \) (still repulsive).
questions.hint: Track each sphere's charge after every contact.
distractor_logic: Halves both charges, ignoring that C already carries charge when it reaches B.
Halves only A's charge and leaves B unchanged.
Uses B's new charge but forgets that A was halved.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Charges \( +q,\,+q,\,+q \) and \( -q \) sit at the corners of a square of side \( a \). A charge \( +Q \) is placed at the centre. Find the net force on it.
options: Zero, by the symmetry of the square
questions.explanation:
Each corner is \( a/\sqrt2 \) from the centre, so each force has magnitude \( \dfrac{kqQ}{a^{2}/2}=\dfrac{2kqQ}{a^{2}} \).

The two \( +q \) charges on one diagonal cancel.

On the other diagonal, \( -q \) attracts and the opposite \( +q \) repels, both toward \( -q \): net \( 4kqQ/a^{2} \).
questions.hint: Pair up opposite corners.
distractor_logic: Assumes full cancellation, ignoring that one corner charge has the opposite sign.
Counts only the attraction toward \( -q \), missing the push from the \( +q \) opposite it.
Reverses the direction; \( +Q \) is attracted to \( -q \) and repelled by the charge opposite it.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Equal charges \( +q \) sit at the three corners of an equilateral triangle. Each corner is a distance \( r \) from the centroid. What is the field at the centroid?
questions.explanation:
Each field has magnitude \( kq/r^{2} \), and they point away from their corners, \( 120^\circ \) apart.

Three equal vectors at \( 120^\circ \) sum to zero.
questions.hint: Three equal vectors spaced \( 120^\circ \) apart.
distractor_logic: Adds three magnitudes instead of three vectors \( 120^\circ \) apart.
Cancels two fields directly and leaves the third, but no two of them are antiparallel.
Treats two fields as parallel and the third as opposing.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A square of side \( a \) has \( +q \) at its two top corners and \( -q \) at its two bottom corners. What is the field at the centre?
options: Zero, since the net charge is zero
\( 4\sqrt{2}\,kq/a^{2} \), directed from the bottom side toward the top side
\( 8kq/a^{2} \), directed from the top side toward the bottom side
\( 4\sqrt{2}\,kq/a^{2} \), directed from the top side toward the bottom side
questions.explanation:
Each charge is \( a/\sqrt2 \) away, giving \( 2kq/a^{2} \) each.

Along each diagonal, the \( +q \) (pushing away) and the opposite \( -q \) (pulling toward) add: \( 4kq/a^{2} \) along that diagonal toward the \( -q \) corner.

The two diagonal resultants are perpendicular; their sum is \( 4\sqrt2\,kq/a^{2} \), pointing straight from the \( +q \) side to the \( -q \) side.
questions.hint: Work diagonal by diagonal, then add two perpendicular vectors.
distractor_logic: Zero net charge does not make the field zero at a point.
Reverses the fields; they point away from \( +q \) and toward \( -q \).
Adds the two diagonal resultants as if parallel; they are perpendicular.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Point P is at the origin. Charges of \( +9 \) nC sit at \( (3\text{ m},0) \) and at \( (0,3\text{ m}) \). Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), find the field at P.
options: \( 9\sqrt{2} \) N/C, directed away from both charges, at \( 45^\circ \) between the \( -x \) and \( -y \) directions
\( 18 \) N/C, directed away from both charges, at \( 45^\circ \) between the \( -x \) and \( -y \) directions
\( 9\sqrt{2} \) N/C, directed toward the midpoint of the line joining the charges
\( 27\sqrt{2} \) N/C, directed away from both charges, at \( 45^\circ \) between the \( -x \) and \( -y \) directions
questions.explanation:
Each field: \( \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times9\times10^{-9}}{3^{2}}=9 \) N/C.
