The charge on the x-axis gives a field along \( -x \); the one on the y-axis gives a field along \( -y \).

Resultant: \( \sqrt{9^{2}+9^{2}}=9\sqrt2 \) N/C at \( 45^\circ \) between \( -x \) and \( -y \).
questions.hint: The two fields are perpendicular; use Pythagoras.
distractor_logic: Adds the two perpendicular fields as plain numbers.
Reverses both field directions; positive charges' fields point away from them.
Divides by \( r \) instead of \( r^{2} \) for each field.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: An electron (charge \( -e \), mass \( m \)) enters a uniform field \( E \) with speed \( v \) perpendicular to the field. How far is it deflected after travelling a distance \( L \) along its original direction?
questions.explanation:
Acceleration across the field: \( a=eE/m \), directed opposite to \( \vec E \).

Time to cover \( L \): \( t=L/v \).

Deflection \( y=\tfrac12at^{2}=\dfrac{eEL^{2}}{2mv^{2}} \).
questions.hint: Treat it like horizontal projectile motion with \( a=eE/m \).
distractor_logic: Forgets the electron's negative charge, which makes the force oppose \( \vec E \).
Drops the \( \tfrac12 \) from \( s=\tfrac12at^{2} \).
Uses \( t \) in place of \( t^{2} \), giving a dimensionally wrong result.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: An electron and a proton are placed in the same uniform field. What is the ratio of the electron's acceleration to the proton's, and how are the accelerations directed?
questions.explanation:
Both feel a force of magnitude \( eE \), opposite in direction.

\( a=eE/m \), so \( a_e/a_p=m_p/m_e\approx1836 \).
questions.hint: Same force magnitude, different masses.
distractor_logic: Equal forces do not give equal accelerations for unequal masses.
Inverts the mass ratio; the lighter electron accelerates more.
Forgets that opposite charges feel opposite forces.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Charges \( +q \) sit at five of the six corners of a regular hexagon of side \( a \); the sixth corner is empty. What is the field at the centre?
options: Zero, by the symmetry of the hexagon
\( kq/a^{2} \), directed away from the empty corner
\( kq/a^{2} \), directed toward the empty corner
questions.explanation:
With all six charges, the field at the centre would be zero.

So the five charges give minus the field that the sixth would have produced.

That missing charge (distance \( a \)) would give \( kq/a^{2} \) pointing away from its corner, so the actual field is \( kq/a^{2} \) toward the empty corner.
questions.hint: Complete the hexagon, then subtract the missing charge's field.
distractor_logic: Full symmetry is broken by the missing charge.
Reverses the direction of the leftover field.
Adds all five magnitudes instead of using vector cancellation.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole consists of \( \pm5 \) nC separated by 2 mm. Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\), find the field at a point on its axis 0.1 m from its centre.
options: \( 180 \) N/C, in the direction of \( \vec p \)
\( 90 \) N/C, in the direction of \( \vec p \)
\( 18 \) N/C, in the direction of \( \vec p \)
questions.hint: Find \( p \) first, then use the axial far-field formula.
distractor_logic: Uses the equatorial formula (no factor 2) for an axial point.
Reverses the axial direction; on the axis the field is along \( \vec p \).
Divides by \( r^{2} \) instead of \( r^{3} \).

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A point A on the axis of a short dipole and a point B on its equatorial line have fields of equal magnitude. What is the ratio of their distances from the dipole's centre, \( r_A/r_B \)?
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{2kp}{r_A^{3}}=\dfrac{kp}{r_B^{3}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{r_A^{3}}{r_B^{3}}=2 \).

So \( r_A/r_B=2^{1/3} \): the axial point must be farther away.
questions.hint: Set the two far-field expressions equal.
distractor_logic: Swaps the axial and equatorial formulas.
Ignores the cube in the \( 1/r^{3} \) law.
Uses a \( 1/r^{2} \) dependence.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole with separation 2 cm feels a torque of \( 4\times10^{-3} \) N m when at \( 30^\circ \) to a uniform field of \( 1\times10^{5} \) N/C. What is the magnitude of each charge?
questions.explanation:
\( p=\dfrac{\tau}{E\sin\theta}=\dfrac{4\times10^{-3}}{10^{5}\times\tfrac12}=8\times10^{-8} \) C m.

\( q=\dfrac{p}{2a}=\dfrac{8\times10^{-8}}{0.02}=4\times10^{-6} \) C \( =4\,\mu \)C.
questions.hint: Get \( p \) from the torque, then divide by the full separation.
distractor_logic: Divides \( p \) by \( a=1 \) cm instead of the full separation \( 2a=2 \) cm.
Ignores \( \sin30^\circ \), taking the torque as maximum.
Uses 2 m instead of 0.02 m for the separation.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A dipole of moment \( 2\times10^{-8} \) C m is in a uniform field of \( 5\times10^{4} \) N/C. How much work must an external agent do to turn it slowly from \( 60^\circ \) to \( 180^\circ \)?
questions.explanation:
\( pE=(2\times10^{-8})(5\times10^{4})=1\times10^{-3} \) J.

\( W=U_f-U_i=-pE\cos180^\circ+pE\cos60^\circ=pE(1+\tfrac12) \).

\( W=1.5\times10^{-3} \) J.
questions.hint: Work by the agent equals \( U_f-U_i \) with \( U=-pE\cos\theta \).
distractor_logic: Stops at \( 90^\circ \) instead of going to \( 180^\circ \).
Starts from \( 0^\circ \) instead of \( 60^\circ \).
Gives the work done by the field, not by the external agent.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A short dipole sits near a fixed positive point charge \( +Q \), with \( \vec p \) pointing directly away from \( Q \). What does the dipole experience?
options: A net force toward \( Q \), and no torque
A net force away from \( Q \), and no torque
A torque but no net force
Neither a force nor a torque, since its net charge is zero
questions.explanation:
With \( \vec p \) pointing away from \( Q \), the \( -q \) end is nearer \( Q \), where the field is stronger.

The attraction on \( -q \) exceeds the repulsion on \( +q \): net force toward \( Q \).

\( \vec p \) is parallel to the local field, so there is no torque.
questions.hint: Which end sits in the stronger field?
distractor_logic: Weights the \( +q \) end more, but that end is farther from \( Q \) where the field is weaker.
Applies the uniform-field result to a non-uniform field.
Zero net charge does not guarantee zero force in a non-uniform field.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: Two identical dipoles, each of moment \( p \), are placed at the same point with their moments perpendicular to each other. What is the net dipole moment?
options: \( 2p \), along the bisector of the angle between the two moments
\( \sqrt{2}\,p \), along the bisector of the angle between the two moments
\( \sqrt{2}\,p \), perpendicular to the bisector of the angle between the two moments
questions.explanation:
Dipole moments add as vectors.

Two equal perpendicular vectors give \( \sqrt{p^{2}+p^{2}}=\sqrt2\,p \), along the bisector.
questions.hint: Add the moments as vectors.
distractor_logic: Adds the magnitudes as if the moments were parallel.
Only antiparallel moments cancel; perpendicular ones do not.
Right magnitude, but the resultant of two equal perpendicular vectors lies along their bisector.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A uniform field \( \vec E=3\times10^{3}\,\hat i \) N/C passes through a square of side 10 cm whose plane makes \( 60^\circ \) with the x-axis. Find the flux through the square.
questions.explanation:
The plane makes \( 60^\circ \) with \( \vec E \), so the normal makes \( 30^\circ \) with it.

\( \Phi=EA\cos30^\circ=3\times10^{3}\times0.01\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=15\sqrt3 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.
questions.hint: Convert the angle with the plane into the angle with the normal.
distractor_logic: Uses \( 60^\circ \) as the angle with the normal; the normal makes \( 30^\circ \) with the x-axis.
Ignores the tilt of the square.
Right number, but N/C is the unit of field, not flux.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A field \( \vec E=(2\hat i+3\hat j)\times10^{2} \) N/C passes through a flat area of 0.5 m\(^{2}\) lying in the yz-plane. What is the flux through it?
questions.explanation:
A surface in the yz-plane has its area vector along \( \hat i \).

\( \Phi=\vec E\cdot\vec A=(2\times10^{2})(0.5)=100 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C; the \( \hat j \) part contributes nothing.
questions.hint: Only the component along the area vector counts.
distractor_logic: Uses the y-component, which runs parallel to the surface.
Adds the components as plain numbers.
Uses the full magnitude \( |\vec E| \) instead of the normal component.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A thin ring of radius \( R \) carries a uniformly distributed charge \( Q \). What is the field at its centre?
options: \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 R} \), as for a long wire
\( \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^{2}} \), perpendicular to the plane of the ring
questions.explanation:
Split the ring into small elements. Each element has an identical element diametrically opposite.

Their fields at the centre are equal and opposite, so all contributions cancel: \( E=0 \).
questions.hint: Pair each small element with the one directly opposite it.
distractor_logic: Treats the whole charge as a point charge at distance \( R \), ignoring cancellation.
Borrows the infinite-line formula for a closed ring.
The element fields at the centre lie in the ring's plane, so they cannot produce a perpendicular field.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: For a closed surface, the flux entering is 30 N m\(^{2}\)/C and the flux leaving is 50 N m\(^{2}\)/C. What is the net flux, and what can you say about the enclosed charge?
options: \( +80 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C; the net enclosed charge is positive
\( +20 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C; the net enclosed charge is positive
\( -20 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C; the net enclosed charge is negative
\( +20 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C; nothing can be said about the enclosed charge
questions.explanation:
Leaving flux counts positive, entering negative: \( \Phi=50-30=+20 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.

A positive net outward flux means more lines start inside than end inside: net positive charge enclosed.
questions.hint: Outward flux is positive by convention.
distractor_logic: Adds entering and leaving flux as magnitudes.
Reverses the sign convention; leaving flux is positive.
Net flux is directly proportional to the enclosed charge, so its sign tells us the charge's sign.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A thin spherical shell carries a fixed charge \( Q \) uniformly. If its radius is doubled with \( Q \) unchanged, its surface charge density becomes
questions.explanation:
\( \sigma=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi R^{2}} \).

Doubling \( R \) multiplies the area by 4, so \( \sigma \) falls to \( \sigma/4 \).
questions.hint: Surface density is charge divided by \( 4\pi R^{2} \).
distractor_logic: Scales area linearly with radius.
Uses the volume scaling \( R^{3} \) for a surface density.
Inverts the scaling; spreading the same charge over more area lowers \( \sigma \).

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A uniform field of \( 5\times10^{3} \) N/C makes an angle of \( 30^\circ \) with the plane of a flat rectangle measuring 0.2 m by 0.1 m. Find the flux through the rectangle.
questions.explanation:
Angle with the plane is \( 30^\circ \), so the angle with the normal is \( 60^\circ \).

\( \Phi=EA\cos60^\circ=5\times10^{3}\times0.02\times\tfrac12=50 \) N m\(^{2}\)/C.
questions.hint: Flux uses the angle with the normal, not with the surface.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \cos30^\circ \), treating the angle with the plane as the angle with the normal.
Ignores the angle altogether.
Uses the perimeter (0.6 m) instead of the area.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: Two large parallel sheets carry uniform densities \( +\sigma \) and \( -\sigma \). What is the field between them and outside them?
options: \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) between them (from the \( +\sigma \) sheet toward the \( -\sigma \) sheet); zero outside
\( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) between them (from the \( -\sigma \) sheet toward the \( +\sigma \) sheet); zero outside
questions.explanation:
Each sheet gives \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \).

Between the sheets both fields point from \( +\sigma \) toward \( -\sigma \): they add to \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \).

Outside they point oppositely and cancel.
questions.hint: Superpose two \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) fields region by region.
distractor_logic: This is the pattern for two sheets of the same sign.
Uses the single-sheet field between them, forgetting the second sheet adds.
Reverses the direction; field points away from positive and toward negative charge.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: Two large parallel sheets both carry uniform density \( +\sigma \). What is the field between them and outside them?
options: Zero between them; \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) outside, pointing away from the sheets
\( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) everywhere, pointing away from the nearer sheet
Zero between them; \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) outside, pointing toward the sheets
questions.explanation:
Each sheet gives \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) pointing away from it.

Between them the two fields oppose and cancel.

Outside they point the same way and add to \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \).
questions.hint: In each region, check whether the two sheets' fields point the same way.
distractor_logic: This is the pattern for oppositely charged sheets.
Treats each region as feeling only one sheet.
Reverses direction; positive sheets' fields point away from them.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A point charge \( q \) is placed at one corner of a cube. What is the total flux through the cube?
questions.explanation:
Eight identical cubes can be arranged around the corner to enclose the charge fully.

By symmetry each gets one-eighth of \( q/\epsilon_0 \): \( q/8\epsilon_0 \).
questions.hint: How many such cubes would completely surround the charge?
distractor_logic: Assumes the whole charge is enclosed.
Uses the centre-of-cube result for one face.
Assumes a quarter of the space surrounds the corner.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: Concentric thin shells of radii \( a \) and \( b \) (\( a<b \)) carry charges \( Q_1 \) and \( Q_2 \). What is the field at a distance \( r \) with \( a<r<b \)? (\( Q_1>0 \))
questions.explanation:
Take a Gaussian sphere of radius \( r \) between the shells. It encloses only \( Q_1 \).

\( E\cdot4\pi r^{2}=Q_1/\epsilon_0 \Rightarrow E=\dfrac{Q_1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \); the outer shell contributes nothing inside itself.
questions.hint: Which shell does your Gaussian sphere enclose?
distractor_logic: Includes the outer shell, whose charge is not enclosed.
Counts the outer shell instead of the inner one.
Applies the inside-a-shell result, but the inner shell's charge is enclosed.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: The field 2 cm from an infinitely long, uniformly charged wire is \( 9\times10^{4} \) N/C. Taking \( k=9\times10^{9} \) N m\(^{2}\)/C\(^{2}\) and \( E=2k\lambda/r \), find the linear charge density.
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{Er}{2k}=\dfrac{9\times10^{4}\times0.02}{2\times9\times10^{9}} \).

\( \lambda=\dfrac{1.8\times10^{3}}{1.8\times10^{10}}=1\times10^{-7} \) C/m.
questions.hint: Rearrange the line-charge formula for \( \lambda \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( E=k\lambda/r \), dropping the factor 2.
Uses \( E=2k\lambda/r^{2} \), a point-charge-like dependence.
Substitutes 2 m instead of 0.02 m.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A point charge \( q \) is held a distance \( a/2 \) directly above the centre of a square of side \( a \). What is the flux through the square?
questions.explanation:
The square is one face of a cube of side \( a \) centred on the charge.

The cube's total flux is \( q/\epsilon_0 \), shared equally by 6 faces: \( q/6\epsilon_0 \).
questions.hint: Build an imaginary cube around the charge.
distractor_logic: The square alone is not a closed surface enclosing the charge.
Assumes the square catches half of all the flux, as an infinite plane would.
Uses the corner-of-cube result.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: The field at point P due to a positive charge Q is \( 2\times10^{4} \) N/C, directed away from Q. A charge of \( -3\,\mu \)C is placed at P. What force acts on it?
questions.explanation:
\( \vec F=q\vec E \), so \( F=(3\times10^{-6})(2\times10^{4})=6\times10^{-2} \) N.

\( q \) is negative, so the force is opposite to \( \vec E \), i.e. toward Q, as expected for unlike charges attracting.
questions.hint: The field already encodes Coulomb's law; just multiply by the signed charge.
distractor_logic: Forgets that a negative charge feels a force opposite to \( \vec E \); unlike charges attract.
Confuses the field value with the force.
Ignores the micro-prefix on the charge.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: At what distance \( r \) from a point charge \( q \) is its field equal in magnitude to the field of an infinite plane sheet with surface density \( \sigma \)?
options: No such distance exists, since the sheet's field does not depend on distance
questions.explanation:
Set \( \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0} \).

\( r^{2}=\dfrac{q}{2\pi\sigma} \Rightarrow r=\sqrt{\dfrac{q}{2\pi\sigma}} \).
questions.hint: Equate the point-charge field to \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \).
distractor_logic: Uses the conductor field \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) instead of \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \) for the sheet.
Forgets to take the square root after equating.
A varying field can equal a constant one at one particular distance.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A closed surface S1 encloses an entire dipole (\( +q \) and \( -q \)). Another closed surface S2 encloses only its \( +q \) charge. What are the fluxes through S1 and S2?
options: Zero through S1 and \( q/\epsilon_0 \) through S2
\( 2q/\epsilon_0 \) through S1 and \( q/\epsilon_0 \) through S2
Zero through both S1 and S2
\( q/\epsilon_0 \) through both S1 and S2
questions.explanation:
Gauss's law uses net enclosed charge.

S1: \( q_{enc}=+q-q=0 \), so zero flux. S2: \( q_{enc}=+q \), so flux \( q/\epsilon_0 \).
questions.hint: Count the signed charge inside each surface.
distractor_logic: Adds the magnitudes of the two charges instead of their signed values.
Assumes a dipole's field produces no flux anywhere; S2 encloses a net charge.
Forgets that S1 also encloses the \( -q \) charge.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A thin rod 0.5 m long carries a uniform linear charge density of \( +3.2\times10^{-9} \) C/m. How many electrons does this charge correspond to, and were they added or removed? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
\( Q=\lambda L=(3.2\times10^{-9})(0.5)=1.6\times10^{-9} \) C.

\( n=Q/e=\dfrac{1.6\times10^{-9}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=1\times10^{10} \); positive charge means electrons were removed.
questions.hint: Total charge first (\( \lambda L \)), then count electrons.
distractor_logic: Adding electrons would make the rod negative.
Divides \( \lambda \) by \( e \) directly, forgetting to multiply by the length.
Divides \( \lambda \) by the length instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: An electron (mass \( m \)) is released near a large plane sheet with uniform positive density \( \sigma \). What is its acceleration?
options: \( \dfrac{e\sigma}{\epsilon_0 m} \), constant, directed toward the sheet
\( \dfrac{e\sigma}{2\epsilon_0 m} \), constant, directed away from the sheet
\( \dfrac{e\sigma}{2\epsilon_0 m} \), constant, directed toward the sheet
Decreasing as \( 1/r^{2} \), directed toward the sheet
questions.explanation:
The sheet's field is uniform: \( E=\sigma/2\epsilon_0 \), pointing away from it.

Force on the electron \( eE \) is toward the sheet; \( a=\dfrac{eE}{m}=\dfrac{e\sigma}{2\epsilon_0 m} \), constant.
questions.hint: Sheet field is uniform; the electron's charge is negative.
distractor_logic: Uses the conductor-surface field \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) for a thin sheet.
Forgets that the negative electron is pulled toward the positive sheet.
Treats the sheet like a point charge; its field does not weaken with distance.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A short dipole \( \vec p \) is at distance \( r \) from a point charge \( +Q \) (\( r \) much larger than the dipole's length), with \( \vec p \) perpendicular to the line joining them. What is the magnitude of the torque on the dipole?
options: Zero, since a point charge's field is not uniform
questions.explanation:
Over the small dipole, the field of \( Q \) is nearly uniform: \( E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \).

\( \vec p \perp \vec E \), so \( \tau=pE\sin90^\circ=\dfrac{pQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \).
questions.hint: Find the point charge's field at the dipole, then use \( \tau=pE\sin\theta \).
distractor_logic: Non-uniformity adds a net force but does not remove the torque.
Uses the dipole's own field formula instead of the field of \( Q \).
Uses a \( 1/r \) field for a point charge.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: Two large parallel sheets carry densities \( +\sigma \) and \( -\sigma \). What is the force per unit area on the \( -\sigma \) sheet?
options: Zero, since the field outside the pair is zero
questions.explanation:
The force on a sheet comes only from the OTHER sheet's field: \( \sigma/2\epsilon_0 \).

Force per area \( =\sigma\times\dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}=\dfrac{\sigma^{2}}{2\epsilon_0} \), attractive since the charges are opposite.
questions.hint: Exclude the sheet's own field when finding the force on it.
distractor_logic: Uses the total field between the sheets, which includes the sheet's own field; a sheet cannot push itself.
Opposite charges attract, they do not repel.
The \( -\sigma \) sheet sits in the field of the \( +\sigma \) sheet, which is not zero.

questions.topic: Continuous Charge Distributions and Electric Flux
questions.question: A field \( \vec E=\alpha x\,\hat i \) exists in space. A cube of side \( a \) occupies \( a\le x\le2a \) with faces parallel to the coordinate planes. What charge does it enclose?
questions.explanation:
Only the faces at \( x=a \) and \( x=2a \) carry flux.

\( \Phi=(2\alpha a)a^{2}-(\alpha a)a^{2}=\alpha a^{3} \).

Gauss: \( q_{enc}=\epsilon_0\Phi=\epsilon_0\alpha a^{3} \).
questions.hint: Flux out of the far face minus flux into the near face.
distractor_logic: Adds the magnitudes of the flux through the two x-faces instead of subtracting.
Treats the field as uniform, so that entering and leaving flux would match.
Divides by \( \epsilon_0 \) instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: A thin ring of radius \( R \) carries uniform positive density \( \lambda \), except for a tiny gap of length \( d \) (\( d\ll R \)). What is the field at the centre?
options: Zero, by the symmetry of the ring
\( \dfrac{\lambda d}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^{2}} \), directed away from the gap
\( \dfrac{\lambda d}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^{2}} \), directed toward the gap
questions.explanation:
A full ring gives zero at the centre. The gapped ring equals full ring minus the missing piece \( \lambda d \).

That piece alone would give \( \dfrac{\lambda d}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^{2}} \) pointing away from the gap, so the gapped ring gives the same magnitude toward the gap.
questions.hint: Full ring minus a small point-like piece.
distractor_logic: The gap breaks the symmetry; a complete ring would give zero.
Reverses the direction of the leftover field.
Uses the infinite-line formula instead of the missing point-like piece.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Which of these fields falls off fastest with distance?
options: The field of a point charge
The field of an infinite line charge
The field of an infinite plane sheet
The far field of an electric dipole
questions.explanation:
Sheet: independent of \( r \). Line: \( 1/r \). Point charge: \( 1/r^{2} \).

Dipole far field: \( 1/r^{3} \), the fastest, because the two charges' fields nearly cancel far away.
questions.hint: Compare the powers of \( r \).
distractor_logic: Falls as \( 1/r^{2} \), slower than the dipole's \( 1/r^{3} \).
Falls only as \( 1/r \).
Does not fall off at all.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A drop of mass \( 4.8\times10^{-15} \) kg is held stationary by an upward field of \( 1\times10^{5} \) N/C. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\(^{2}\) and \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C, what can you say about its charge?
options: Its charge is \( 4.8\times10^{-19} \) C, which is not a whole number of electrons
questions.explanation:
\( qE=mg \Rightarrow q=\dfrac{4.8\times10^{-15}\times10}{10^{5}}=4.8\times10^{-19} \) C.

The force must be upward along the upward field, so \( q>0 \). \( n=q/e=3 \): three electrons lost.
questions.hint: Balance \( qE \) against \( mg \), then divide by \( e \).
distractor_logic: A negative drop would be pushed down by an upward field.
Multiplies the weight by \( E \) instead of dividing.
\( 4.8\times10^{-19} \) C is exactly \( 3e \), so quantization is satisfied.

questions.topic: Gauss's Law and Its Applications
questions.question: A solid metal conductor carries a net charge and is in electrostatic equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: The field inside the metal equals \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \)
The field is zero inside the metal, and just outside it is normal to the surface
Just outside the surface the field is tangential to it
The charge spreads uniformly through the whole volume
questions.explanation:
Any field inside would move free electrons, so equilibrium needs \( E=0 \) inside; Gauss's law then puts all excess charge on the surface.

Any tangential component at the surface would also move charges, so the outside field must be normal.
questions.hint: Equilibrium means no charge is moving.
distractor_logic: \( \sigma/\epsilon_0 \) is the field just outside; inside it is zero.
A tangential component would move charges along the surface, contradicting equilibrium.
Excess charge on a conductor resides on its surface.

questions.topic: Electric Dipole: Dipole Field and Torque in a Uniform External Field
questions.question: A small dipole is placed at the centre of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell. What does the shell's charge do to the dipole?
options: It exerts a torque \( pE\sin\theta \) with \( E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^{2}} \)
No torque, but a net force toward the shell
Nothing: no torque and no net force, since the shell's field inside is zero
Maximum torque, since the field inside is radial
questions.explanation:
By Gauss's law the shell's field is zero everywhere inside it.

With \( E=0 \), both the torque \( pE\sin\theta \) and any net force vanish.
questions.hint: What field does a charged shell produce inside itself?
distractor_logic: Uses the surface value of the field for a point inside the shell.
There is no field inside to produce any force.
The field inside the shell is zero, not radial.

questions.topic: Electric Charge: Properties, Quantization, and Conservation; Coulomb's Law
questions.question: A point charge \( q \) sits at the centre of a thin shell of radius \( R \) carrying charge \( Q \). What is the field at \( r>R \), and what force does the shell exert on \( q \)?
options: \( \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \) outside; the force on \( q \) is zero
\( \dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \) outside; the force on \( q \) is \( \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^{2}} \)
\( \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \) outside; the force on \( q \) is zero
\( \dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \) outside; the force on \( q \) is zero
questions.explanation:
A Gaussian sphere with \( r>R \) encloses \( Q+q \), giving \( E=\dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^{2}} \).

Inside the shell, its own field is zero, so it exerts no force on \( q \).
questions.hint: Enclosed charge outside; shell field inside.
distractor_logic: Forgets that the centre charge is also enclosed by a Gaussian sphere outside.
The shell's field inside is zero, so it exerts no force on \( q \).
Forgets the shell's own charge in the enclosed total.

questions.topic: Electric Field Due to Point Charges and Systems of Charges; Electric Field Lines
questions.question: Why does the far field of a dipole fall off faster than that of a single point charge?
options: Far away, the fields of \( +q \) and \( -q \) nearly cancel, leaving a small residue that falls as \( 1/r^{3} \)
Because the dipole's net charge is \( 2q \), which spreads the field over more space
Because a dipole's field exists only in the region between its two charges
Because the dipole moment itself decreases with distance from the dipole
questions.explanation:
